Machine Learning: Personal Loan Campaign¶

Description¶

Context¶

AllLife Bank is a mid-sized, fast-growing US-based financial institution that offers a range of retail banking services, including savings and checking accounts, fixed deposits, and personal loans. The bank’s business model is centered on building long-term customer relationships, expanding its retail footprint, and growing its loan portfolio to drive sustainable profitability through interest income.

It currently relies on a large base of liability customers (depositors) but faces a significant under-representation of asset customers (borrowers). To drive profitability through interest income, the bank must aggressively expand its loan portfolio by converting existing depositors into personal loan customers.

Last year’s pilot campaign achieved a 9% conversion rate, validating the potential of this strategy. However, to optimize marketing spend and improve efficiency, the retail marketing department requires a more data-driven approach. Enhancing the success ratio of these campaigns is critical for sustainable growth and maximizing customer lifetime value.

Objective¶

The objective is to develop a predictive classification model that identifies patterns and key factors driving personal loan adoption among existing liability customers. By uncovering the demographic and behavioral drivers of loan conversion, the goal is to enable targeted segmentation and more precise marketing interventions that improve campaign conversion rates, optimize marketing spend, and enhance overall profitability through higher-quality loan portfolio growth.

Data Dictionary¶

  • ID: Customer ID
  • Age: Customer’s age in completed years
  • Experience: # years of professional experience
  • Income: Annual income of the customer (in thousand dollars)
  • ZIP Code: Home Address ZIP code.
  • Family: The family size of the customer
  • CCAvg: Average spending on credit cards per month (in thousand dollars)
  • Education: Education Level. 1: Undergrad; 2: Graduate;3: Advanced/Professional
  • Mortgage: Value of house mortgage if any. (in thousand dollars)
  • Personal_Loan: Did this customer accept the personal loan offered in the last campaign?
  • Securities_Account: Does the customer have a securities account with the bank?
  • CD_Account: Does the customer have a certificate of deposit (CD) account with the bank?
  • Online: Do customers use Internet banking facilities?
  • CreditCard: Does the customer use a credit card issued by any other Bank (excluding All Life Bank)?

Domain Details¶

  • Retail Banking Services - The suite of offerings provided by AllLife Bank to its individual customers, including accounts and loans
  • Personal Loan - A personal loan is an unsecured loan provided by financial institutions that does not require any form of collateral
  • Fixed Deposit - A financial product offered by the bank that represents long-term savings held for a specific period
  • Depositers - Customers who hold financial assets within the bank, such as savings, checking accounts, or fixed deposits.
  • Borrowers - Customers who have taken out personal loans from the bank.
  • Asset Customers - A term used to describe borrowers, representing the segment the bank is currently seeking to grow to improve its loan portfolio.
  • Liability Customers - Existing customers (depositors) who hold accounts with the bank, representing the bank's current, large customer base.
  • Loan Business - The bank's operational focus on expanding its loan portfolio to generate revenue.
  • Loan Interest - The revenue generated by the bank from the interest income on its loan portfolio.
  • Interest Rate - The percentage rate charged by the bank on personal loans, which contributes to the bank's sustainable profitability.
  • Securities Account - An account held at a financial institution that allows the holder to hold financial assets like stocks or bonds.
  • Certificate of deposit - A financial product similar to a fixed deposit, where a sum of money is held for a fixed term with an interest rate

Univariate Analysis¶

Numerical (continuous) variables and histogram¶

In [277]:
# Numerical (continuous) variables and histogram
# Plot figure size
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 10))

# Create the list of continuous numerical features for plot histogram to check the distribution and skewness of dataset
num_features = ['Age', 'Experience', 'Income', 'CCAvg', 'Family', 'Mortgage']

# Create the histplot for each numerical feature
for i, feature in enumerate(num_features):
    plt.subplot(3, 3, i+1)
    sns.histplot(data[feature], kde=True)
    plt.title(feature)
    plt.tight_layout()

Observations¶

  • Age and Experience: Both 'Age' and 'Experience' columns show a relatively normal distribution, with values spread across the range without significant skewness or extreme outliers after the negative experience values were handled.
  • Income: The 'Income' distribution is right-skewed, indicating that a majority of customers have lower to moderate incomes, while a smaller proportion of customers have significantly higher incomes.
  • CCAvg (Average spending on credit cards): This variable is also highly right-skewed, suggesting that most customers have low credit card spending. There are a few customers with much higher spending habits, pulling the mean to the right.
  • Family: The 'Family' variable appears to be discrete rather than continuous, with distinct peaks at 1, 2, 3, and 4. Most customers have smaller family sizes.
  • Mortgage: The 'Mortgage' distribution is heavily right-skewed, with a large number of customers having a mortgage value of zero. For customers with mortgages, the values vary widely.

Numerical (continuous) variables and box plots¶

In [278]:
# Numerical (continuous) variables and box plots
# Plot figure size
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 10))

Observations of Numerical (Continuous) Variables (Box Plots)¶

  • Age: The box plot for 'Age' shows a relatively symmetrical distribution with no significant outliers, indicating a consistent spread of ages among customers.
  • Experience: Similar to 'Age', the 'Experience' box plot is also quite symmetrical, and after handling negative values, it appears to have no prominent outliers.
  • Income: The 'Income' box plot clearly displays numerous outliers on the higher end, confirming the right-skewed nature observed in histograms. The median income is relatively low compared to the maximum values, indicating a significant portion of customers with lower incomes and a few with very high incomes.
  • CCAvg: This box plot shows a very high concentration of values near zero and many outliers on the upper side, which is consistent with its highly right-skewed histogram. This indicates that most customers have low credit card spending, with a few having exceptionally high spending.
  • Family: The 'Family' box plot shows distinct boxes for each family size (1, 2, 3, 4), which reinforces its discrete nature. There are no outliers, as expected for this type of variable.
  • Mortgage: The 'Mortgage' box plot also reveals a large number of outliers on the higher side, consistent with the right-skewed histogram and the observation that many customers have zero mortgage. For those with mortgages, there's a wide range of values, with some exceptionally high mortgage amounts.

for feature in category_features:
  # Calculate the percentage of each unique value in the feature
  percentages = data[feature].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
  print (f"{feature}: ", end='')
  print (' | '.join([f"{idx}: {val:.2f}%" for idx, val in percentages.
items()])) # Using .2f for two decimal places
  print('\n')

# Set the figure size for the count plots
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 10))

# Create the countplot for each categorical feature
for i, feature in enumerate(category_features):
    plt.subplot(3, 3, i + 1)
    ax = sns.countplot(data=data, x=feature)
    # Get the total number of data points for percentage calculation
    total = len(data)

    # Add percentage labels on top of each bar
    for p in ax.patches:
        # Calculate the percentage for the current bar
        percentage = '{:.1f}%'.format(100 * p.get_height()/total)
        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2
        y = p.get_height()
        plt.annotate(percentage, (x, y), ha='center')
    plt.title(feature)
    plt.tight_layout()

Securities_Account: 0: 89.56% | 1: 10.44%


CD_Account: 0: 93.96% | 1: 6.04%


Online: 1: 59.68% | 0: 40.32%


CreditCard: 0: 70.60% | 1: 29.40%


Personal_Loan: 0: 90.40% | 1: 9.60%


Education: 1: 41.92% | 3: 30.02% | 2: 28.06%


Family: 1: 29.44% | 2: 25.92% | 4: 24.44% | 3: 20.20%

Observations¶

  • Securities_Account: A vast majority of customers (89.56%) do not have a securities account with the bank, while only a small percentage (10.44%) do.
  • CD_Account: Similar to securities accounts, most customers (93.96%) do not have a Certificate of Deposit (CD) account, with a mere 6.04% having one.
  • Online: A larger proportion of customers (59.68%) use internet banking facilities, compared to those who don't (40.32%).
  • CreditCard: The majority of customers (70.60%) do not use a credit card issued by other banks, whereas 29.40% do.
  • Personal_Loan: This is the target variable. A significant imbalance is observed, with only 9.60% of customers having accepted the personal loan offer, while 90.40% have not. This indicates a rare event, which is common in classification problems and might require special handling during model training.
  • Education: The education levels are fairly distributed, with Undergrad (1) being the most common at 41.92%, followed by Advanced/Professional (3) at 30.02%, and Graduate (2) at 28.06%.
  • Family: Customers with a family size of 1 are the most frequent (29.44%), followed closely by family size 2 (25.92%) and 4 (24.44%). Family size 3 is the least common among these categories at 20.20%.

Bivariate Analysis¶

Numerical(continuous) variables and Heatmap correlation plot¶

In [283]:
# Set the figure size for the Correlation Heatmap plot
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
sns.heatmap(data.corr(), annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap='coolwarm')
plt.title('Correlation Heatmap')
plt.show()

Observations¶

  • Strong Positive Correlation: 'Age' and 'Experience' show a very strong positive correlation (0.98). This is expected, as experience naturally increases with age.
  • Moderate Positive Correlation: 'Income' has a moderate positive correlation with 'CCAvg' (0.65) and 'Personal_Loan' (0.50). This suggests that customers with higher incomes tend to spend more on credit cards and are more likely to accept personal loan offers.
  • Weak/No Correlation: Most other variables show weak or negligible correlations with each other, which is generally good for predictive modeling as it reduces multicollinearity issues. For example, 'Family' and 'Mortgage' have very low correlations with 'Personal_Loan'.
  • Target Variable ('Personal_Loan') Correlations: The target variable 'Personal_Loan' shows the strongest positive correlations with 'Income' (0.50), followed by 'Education' (0.14) and 'CCAvg' (0.11). This indicates that income is the most significant factor in predicting personal loan acceptance among the numerical features.
  • Education: 'Education' appears to have a weak positive correlation with 'Personal_Loan', suggesting that higher education levels might slightly increase the likelihood of accepting a loan, but it's not a strong driver.

Age column can be dropped due to the strong correlation between age and experience

plt.xlabel('Mortgage Value (in thousand dollars)')
plt.ylabel('Frequency')

# Mortage Distribution boxplot
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)

plt.title('Mortgage Distribution (Box Plot)')
plt.xlabel('Mortgage Value (in thousand dollars)')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations¶

  • Highly Skewed: The distribution is heavily right-skewed, with a large concentration of customers having a mortgage value of zero.
  • Zero Mortgages: A significant portion of the customer base (as indicated by the tall bar at 0 in the histogram and the bulk of the data near 0 in the box plot) has no mortgage.
  • Outliers: For customers who do have mortgages, there's a wide range of values, and the box plot clearly shows several outliers with exceptionally high mortgage amounts.
  • Patterns: The histogram suggests a rapid decline in frequency as mortgage values increase from zero, indicating fewer customers with higher mortgage values.

Question 4¶

How does a customer's interest in purchasing a loan vary with their education?

In [293]:
# Count plot of Education vs Personal loan analysis
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
ax = sns.countplot(data=data, x='Education', hue='Personal_Loan', palette='viridis')
plt.title('Personal Loan Acceptance by Education Level')
plt.xlabel('Education Level (1: Undergrad, 2: Graduate, 3: Advanced/Professional)')
plt.ylabel('Number of Customers')
plt.xticks(ticks=[0, 1, 2], labels=['Undergrad', 'Graduate', 'Adv/Professional'])

# Add percentage labels on top of each bar within each group
for p in ax.patches:
    height = p.get_height()
    if height > 0:
        # Calculate the total for this 'Education' category to get percentage of loan acceptance within that category
        education_level = int(p.get_x() + 0.5) # Approximate education level from x-coordinate
        personal_loan_status = 1 if '1' in str(p.get_facecolor()) else 0 # Crude way to check hue

        # Need to calculate total for each education level
        if education_level == 0: # Undergrad
            total_for_education = data[data['Education'] == 1].shape[0]
        elif education_level == 1: # Graduate
            total_for_education = data[data['Education'] == 2].shape[0]
        elif education_level == 2: # Advanced/Professional
            total_for_education = data[data['Education'] == 3].shape[0]
        else:
            total_for_education = 1 # Fallback to avoid division by zero

        percentage = '{:.1f}%'.format(100 * height / total_for_education)
        ax.annotate(percentage, (p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2., height),
                    ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=9, color='black')

plt.legend(title='Personal Loan', labels=['No', 'Yes'])
plt.show()

Observations¶

  • Higher Education, Higher Loan Acceptance: Customers with Advanced/Professional and Graduate education levels show a noticeably higher proportion of personal loan acceptance compared to Undergraduates.
    • For Undergraduates, the percentage of loan takers is significantly lower.
    • For Graduate and Advanced/Professional, the proportion of 'Yes' to 'No' for personal loan is visibly larger.
  • Education as a Key Factor: This plot strongly suggests that education level is a significant factor in determining a customer's interest in or eligibility for a personal loan.
  • Targeting Strategy: Marketing efforts for personal loans could be more effectively targeted towards customers with higher education levels, as they exhibit a greater propensity to accept the loan offer.

Split data - Training and Testing data¶

  • Splitting the data into training and testing sets is crucial to evaluate the performance of our machine learning model on unseen data and prevent overfitting.
  • A common split ratio is 70-80% for training and 20-30% for testing. We will determine an appropriate split for our model.
  • Stratification - Given that the target variable Personal_Loan is highly imbalanced (only 9.60% of customers accepted a loan), it is essential to use stratify=y during the split. This ensures that both the training and testing sets maintain the same proportion of loan acceptors as the original dataset, leading to a more reliable model evaluation.
In [298]:

# Split the data in 70:30 ration to train and test data sets
# Stratification ensures the training and test sets having similar distribution of response
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=y)

print("Shape of training set : ", X_train.shape)
print("Shape of test set     : ", X_test.shape, '\n')

Model build - Decision Tree¶

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Model can make wrong predictions as,¶

  • False Positive (FP) - The model incorrectly predicts a customer will take a loan when they actually won't.
  • False Negative (FN) - The model incorrectly predicts a customer won't take a loan when they actually would have.

Which case is more important?¶

  • Losing a potential customer by predicting that the customer will not be taking the personal loan but in reality the customer was going to take the personal loan
  • If model predicts the customer will purchase a personal loan, but in reality if customer does not, Then bank has to bear the money spent on marketing and others.

Reduce Losses?¶

Recall helps prevent the loss of potential high-priority customers, while the F1 score helps optimize for both False Positives and False Negatives.

we are going to use Recall as our model evaluation criteria to reduce the false negatives

  1. Minimize False Negatives - This ensures that qualified potential loan customers are not incorrectly overlooked.

  2. Maximize Customer Reach - This enables the bank to identify and engage the highest possible number of loan-eligible customers.

    The bank would want the recall to be maximized, the greater the recall score is, the higher are the chances of minimizing the False Negatives.

Model Utility Functions¶

  1. model_performance_classification_sklearn function - to check the model performance of models
  2. confusion_matrix_sklearn function - to plot the confusion matrix

model_performance_classification_sklearn¶

In [299]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using sklearn
def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame({
        'Metric': ['Accuracy', 'Recall', 'Precision', 'F1 Score'],
        'Score': [acc, recall, precision, f1]
    })

    return df_perf

confusion_matrix_sklearn¶

In [300]:
# defining a funtion to compute confusion matrix
def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    # confusion matrix
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, pred)

    # create labels for each cell in the confusion matrix with both count and percentage
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))

    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt='')
    plt.ylabel('True label')
    plt.xlabel('Predicted label')
    plt.title('Confusion Matrix')
    plt.show()

Model Performance Summary¶

The model achieved perfect scores on the training set, indicating that it learned the training data extremely well. However, there is a slight drop in performance on the test set, particularly in precision and F1 score, though recall remains high. This suggests potential overfitting to the training data, which is common for unoptimized Decision Trees. The high recall on the test set (93.75%) is a positive sign, as our primary evaluation criterion is to minimize False Negatives.

Model Performance Evaluation and Improvement¶

Decision Tree (With Class Weights)¶

Because of the dataset is imbalanced—with "No Loan" cases significantly outnumbering "Loan Accepted" cases. A standard Decision Tree may become biased toward the majority class. By setting class_weight="balanced", the model assigns greater importance to the minority "Loan Accepted" class, ensuring it is not overlooked during training.

In [308]:
# Create the decision tree model with class_weight hyper parameter
dt2_model = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1, class_weight="balanced")

# Fit the model on the training data
dt2_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

    • F1 Score: 1.0 (100%)

  • Test Set Performance:

    • Recall: 0.9444 (94.44%)
    • Precision: 0.8500 (85.00%)
    • F1 Score: 0.8947 (89.47%)

Model Performance Summary¶

Setting class_weight="balanced" has resulted in a slightly lower accuracy and precision on the test set compared to the default Decision Tree model. However, it has successfully increased the recall score from 93.75% to 94.44%, which is our primary evaluation metric. This indicates that the model is now better at identifying positive cases (customers who will accept the loan), aligning with our objective to minimize false negatives and maximize customer reach. The trade-off in precision suggests a slight increase in false positives, but this is acceptable given our business objective to prioritize identifying potential loan customers.

Visualizing dtree2¶

In [313]:
# Feature names in X_train
feature_names = list(X_train.columns)

# Plotting the decision tree
plt.figure(figsize=(20, 20))
out = tree.plot_tree(dt2_model, feature_names=feature_names, filled=True, fontsize=9, node_ids=False, class_names=None, proportion=True)
plt.title("Decision Tree 2 Visualization")

# Adding arrows in the decision tree
for o in out:
  arrow = o.arrow_patch
  if arrow is not None:
    arrow.set_edgecolor('black')
    arrow.set_linewidth(1.5)
plt.show()

Observations¶

  • Deep Tree (Similar to dtree1): The tree remains deep, still indicating a high level of complexity and potential for overfitting, similar to the dtree1 model.
  • Key Feature (Income): Income continues to be a crucial splitting feature at higher levels, consistent with dtree1 observations.
  • Impact of class_weight: While visually similar in depth, the class_weight="balanced" parameter subtly influences the splitting criteria. It forces the model to pay more attention to the minority class (Personal_Loan=1), which is reflected in the improved recall score on the test set, even if the overall tree structure still looks complex.
  • Pure Leaves/Complexity: Many pure leaf nodes still exist, but the internal decision logic is now biased towards correctly classifying the minority class, which is a key objective for this model.

Decision Tree (Pre-Pruning)¶

Pre-pruning, also known as early stopping, is a technique used to prevent overfitting by restricting the growth of a decision tree during the training process, typically by setting constraints such as maximum tree depth or minimum samples per leaf

Hyperparameter tuning¶

  • Control Over Model Behavior: Hyperparameters serve as essential configuration settings that dictate how a model learns and functions.
  • Manual Configuration: Unlike standard model parameters learned automatically during training, hyperparameters must be explicitly defined beforehand.
  • Enhanced Performance: Precise tuning improves both model accuracy and generalization, ensuring reliable predictions on new data.
In [315]:
# Define the parameters of the tree to iterate over
max_depth_values = np.arange(2, 11, 2)
max_leaf_nodes_values = np.arange(10, 51, 5)
min_samples_split_values = np.arange(10, 51, 5)

# Variables to store best model and its performance
best_estimator = None
best_score_diff = float('inf')
best_test_score = 0.0

# Iterate over the combinations of hyperparameters
for max_depth in max_depth_values:
    for max_leaf_nodes in max_leaf_nodes_values:
        for min_samples_split in min_samples_split_values:
          estimator = DecisionTreeClassifier(
              max_depth=max_depth,
              max_leaf_nodes=max_leaf_nodes,
              min_samples_split=min_samples_split,
              random_state=1,
              class_weight="balanced"
          )

          # Fit the model to training data
          estimator.fit(X_train, y_train)

          # Make predictions on training and test dataset
          y_train_pred = estimator.predict(X_train)
          y_test_pred = estimator.predict(X_test)

          # Calculate the difference between train and test scores
          train_recall_score = recall_score(y_train, y_train_pred)
          test_recall_score = recall_score(y_test, y_test_pred)

          # Calculate the abs difference between training and test F1 scores
          score_diff = abs(train_recall_score - test_recall_score)

          # Update the best estimator and best score if current score having smaller score difference
          if (score_diff < best_score_diff) and (test_recall_score > best_test_score):
              best_estimator = estimator
              best_score_diff = score_diff

print("Best parameters found:")
print(f"max_depth: {best_estimator.max_depth}")
print(f"max_leaf_nodes: {best_estimator.max_leaf_nodes}")
print(f"min_samples_split: {best_estimator.min_samples_split}")
print(f"Best score difference: {best_score_diff}")
print(f"Best test recall score: {best_test_score}")

Model Performance Summary¶

  • Shallow & Interpretable: Significantly shallower and more interpretable than dtree1 and dtree2 due to pre-pruning, indicating reduced overfitting.
  • Generalization Improved: Training metrics (e.g., Accuracy: 0.788, Precision: 0.312) are no longer perfect, a positive sign for better generalization.
  • Perfect Recall: Achieved excellent recall (1.0 for both train/test), effectively identifying all positive loan cases, aligning with the primary business objective.
  • Precision Trade-off: Lower precision (Test: 0.308) and F1 Score (Test: 0.471) indicate more false positives, an acceptable trade-off for maximizing recall.

Decision Tree (Post-Pruning)¶

Tree Size Control: Cost complexity pruning serves as an alternative method for managing the size of a decision tree.

Parameterization: In DecisionTreeClassifier, this technique is controlled by the ccp_alpha cost complexity parameter.

Pruning Intensity: Increasing the value of ccp_alpha results in a higher number of nodes being pruned.

Optimization: This approach is primarily used to demonstrate how ccp_alpha regularizes trees and how to determine its optimal value.

Total Leaf Impurity vs. Effective Alphas: Minimal cost-complexity pruning iteratively identifies and prunes the node with the "weakest link," defined by its effective alpha value; nodes with the smallest effective alphas are removed first.

Determining Appropriate Alphas: To identify suitable ccp_alpha values, scikit-learn provides the cost_complexity_pruning_path method, which calculates the effective alphas and corresponding total leaf impurities at each stage of the pruning process.

Regularization Effect: As the alpha value increases, the tree undergoes more extensive pruning, resulting in higher total leaf impurity.

In [323]:
# Create an instance of decision tree model with class_weight as balanced
clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1, class_weight="balanced")

# Fit the model to training data
path = clf.cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_train, y_train)

# Extract the array of effective alphas and impurities from pruning path
ccp_alphas = abs(path.ccp_alphas)
impurities = path.impurities

  clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1, class_weight="balanced", ccp_alpha=ccp_alpha)

  # Fit the model to training data

  # Append the model to the list
  clfs.append(clf)

Model Performance Summary¶

  • Strong, Consistent Accuracy: The model demonstrates high predictive accuracy (~95%) across both training and testing datasets.

  • Perfect Recall: With a test recall of 1.0, the model successfully identifies every actual positive loan-conversion case.

  • Precision Limitations: The lower precision (~67%) indicates that the model also generates a notable number of false positives.

  • Balanced Reliability: The F1 score (~0.80) represents a solid trade-off between recall and precision, confirming the model is a reliable tool for identifying potential loan customers, despite a tendency toward over-prediction.

Decision Tree (Closer Test & Train alphas)¶

Balancing Complexity and Performance: The alpha parameter serves as a regulator, managing the trade-off between the tree's complexity and its predictive performance.

Selecting the Optimal Alpha: We select the alpha value that minimizes the difference between the testing and training performance metrics, identifying the point where the two align most closely.

Improving Generalization: Models derived from this optimal point (where the gap between train and test alpha is smallest) are expected to generalize more effectively to unseen data.

In [338]:
# Compute the difference in recall between train and test and save in recall_diff
recall_diff = [abs(tr - te) for tr, te in zip(train_recall, test_recall)]

min_diff = min(recall_diff)
min_index = recall_diff.index(min_diff)

# Create the model where we get the highest test F1 score
dt5_model = clfs[min_index]

print(dt5_model)

DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=np.float64(0.023074692478403356),
                       class_weight='balanced', random_state=1)

Observation¶

  • we clearly notice the alpha used is 0.023074692478403356, different from alpha used in post-pruned tree created from max alpha 0.00222
  • This intersection point is also visible in "Recall vs Alpha for training and test data sets" graph

Model Performance Summary¶

Consistent Performance: The results are similar to those achieved with the pre-pruning model.

Perfect Recall (1.0): The model identifies all actual loan buyers, successfully supporting the bank's goal of capturing every potential customer.

Low Precision (~31%): The high volume of false positives suggests that many non-buyers are incorrectly classified as potential customers.

Balanced Trade-off: With an accuracy of ~78% and an F1 score of ~0.47, the model is moderately effective, though it clearly prioritizes recall over precision.

Final Model Selection¶

1. Standard Decision Tree (Default) - Suffers from severe overfitting. While it achieves perfect scores (1.0) on training data, precision on the test set declines to ~89%.

2. Balanced Decision Tree - Exhibits similar overfitting tendencies as the default model. It Shows slightly lower test performance, with recall at ~94% and precision at ~85%. This model is not ideal for production; the high rate of false positives poses a risk of inefficient marketing expenditure.

3. Pre-Pruning Decision Tree - Achieves 100% recall but suffers from very low precision (~31%). While it successfully identifies all potential customers, the high volume of false positives leads to poor targeting efficiency and risks annoying non-interested customers.

4. Post-Pruning Decision Tree (Max Recall) - Provides an excellent balance, maintaining 1.0 recall alongside ~67% precision and an F1 score of ~0.80 on both datasets.

This model offers the best generalization and cost-effectiveness, making it the most suitable candidate for real-world marketing deployment.

5. Post-Pruning Decision Tree (Minimal Recall Difference) - Mirrors the pre-pruning results; while recall is perfect, the precision and F1 scores remain suboptimal.

Similar to the pre-pruning approach, the lack of precision significantly hampers the efficiency of targeted campaigns.

Model Recommendation:¶

The Post-Pruning model optimized for Max Recall is the preferred choice. It effectively balances the need to capture all potential responders while minimizing false positives, ensuring a focused and high-impact marketing strategy.

Key Features for Predicting Loan Acceptance¶

  1. Income (~0.65) - The primary driver of loan acceptance, significantly more influential than any other demographic or behavioral factor.

  2. Credit Card Spending (CCAvg) (~0.10) - The second most critical predictor, indicating that a customer's monthly credit card spend is a reliable indicator of loan interest.

  3. Education Level - A moderate contributor to the model. Higher education categories show higher importance, suggesting that academic background influences the likelihood of accepting a loan.

  4. Household Composition (Family Size) - Household size variables (particularly family size 3, 2, and 4) offer meaningful predictive value, confirming that family structure is a relevant factor for loan behavior.

  5. Geography (ZIP Code) - Negligible impact. Geographic location is a weak predictor of loan acceptance compared to personal financial and family metrics.

  6. Banking Usage & Other Factors - Minimal influence. Factors such as online banking, existing mortgage, security accounts, and work experience have virtually no effect on the model's predictions.

Actionable Insights & Recommendations¶

Business Recommendations¶

  1. Prioritize High-Income Segments: Income is your strongest predictor; target customers earning >$92.5k, as they are most likely to accept personal loan offers.

  2. Use Spending Patterns as a Filter: Utilize average credit card spending (CCAvg >$2.95k) as a secondary filter to refine and sharpen your target lists.

  3. Personalize via Demographics: Tailor marketing messages based on education levels (graduates and professionals) and family size to improve engagement.

  4. Optimize Marketing Spend: Precision is ~67%; avoid "blanket" campaigns. Instead, use model scores to tier customers and focus outreach on those most likely to convert to prevent wasted budget and customer fatigue.

  5. Drive Upsell Strategies: Specifically target deposit-only customers who demonstrate high income and active credit card usage with pre-approved loan offers or preferential interest rates.

Model Limitations & Considerations¶

  1. Behavioral Shifts: The model reflects past data; it may not predict future shifts in spending or income. Regular reviews and model updates are essential.

  2. Data Volume: Incorporating more comprehensive customer data will improve predictive reliability and model performance.

  3. False Positive Management: With a precision of ~67%, roughly 1 in 3 predictions may not convert. Adjust marketing budgets accordingly to account for this margin of error.

  4. Focus on Key Drivers: Ignore low-impact features like ZIP code or mortgage status. Focus all targeting efforts exclusively on income, education, and credit card usage.
